name: Caudate nucleus
summary: A C-shaped mass of gray matter that follows the lateral ventricle: a bulbous head in the wall of the frontal horn, a body along the floor of the ventricle above the thalamus, and a slender tail curving down into the roof of the temporal horn to end near the amygdala. With the putamen (to which it is joined by gray bridges across the anterior limb of the internal capsule) it forms the striatum, the input stage of the basal ganglia. The head receives prefrontal and association cortex and is the substrate of the cognitive and limbic loops; its atrophy flattens the frontal horns in Huntington disease, and lesions cause abulia, executive dysfunction and sometimes chorea rather than weakness.

anatomy.location: Medial to the anterior limb of the internal capsule and lateral to the frontal horn (head), on the floor of the body of the lateral ventricle lateral to the thalamus (body), and in the roof of the temporal horn (tail); supplied by the recurrent artery of Heubner and the lenticulostriate arteries.

subdivisions.name: Head
subdivisions.note: prefrontal, orbitofrontal and cingulate input; cognitive and limbic loops

subdivisions.name: Tail
subdivisions.note: visual and auditory association input; ends at the amygdala

relations.medial: frontal horn and body of the lateral ventricle
relations.lateral: anterior limb of the internal capsule and putamen

function: Input nucleus of the basal ganglia for the associative and limbic loops: goal-directed behavior, learning of habits and reward, cognitive flexibility, eye movement control (caudate → substantia nigra pars reticulata → superior colliculus).

bestView.label: caudate head bulging into the frontal horn
head of the caudate lateral to the frontal horn, medial to the internal capsule

imaging.normalAppearance: The head is the gray matter indenting the lateral wall of the frontal horn on axial and coronal images; the body runs along the ventricular floor. Flattening or concavity of the frontal horn walls (loss of the caudate bulge) is the signature of Huntington disease; symmetric caudate and putamen T2 hyperintensity suggests toxic, metabolic or prion disease.

pathology.finding: Bilateral caudate head atrophy giving boxcar frontal horns, with putaminal atrophy.
Restriction in the caudate head from Heubner's artery or lenticulostriate occlusion; abulia, confusion or contralateral chorea.
Bilateral caudate and putamen DWI hyperintensity (striatal ribbon) with cortical ribboning.
Symmetric striatal T2 change; the globus pallidus is the CO target, the striatum the hypoglycemia target.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of striatal inhibition of the pallidum

examination: Observe for chorea at rest and with distraction (finger counting)
Family history of movement disorder or dementia
pearls: Chorea with personality change and a family history: look at the caudate heads on the scan
Caudate strokes present with behavioral change more than weakness
